Guide Bilge pump removal & installation Difficulty: Beginner Time: ~10 min Applies to: All boards Last updated: Sep 2026 Watch the walkthrough Watch on YouTube ↗ · JETSURF Service Tutorials #12. Timestamps in the steps below follow the video's on-screen counter (0:00–0:51). The bilge pump clears water from the hull. This is one of the easiest jobs on the board — a single bolt holds it in its bracket and there's one connector. Do it if the pump stops moving water or gets noisy. Tools & supplies The tool for the bracket bolt (Allen key or screwdriver, per your model) Replacement bilge pump if you're swapping it Removal 0:00 — Unscrew the bracket bolt. 0:20 — Carefully slide the pump out of the bracket and disconnect the connector. Installation 0:33 — Connect the connector. 0:51 — Slide the pump into the bracket and secure it with the bolt. Tip: before you refit, clear any hair or grit from the pump inlet screen and check the outlet hose is still seated — that's usually why a pump "stops working." Caution: seat the pump fully in its bracket before tightening the bolt so it can't vibrate loose, and make sure the connector clicks home — a half-seated connector corrodes. Timestamps below follow the video's on-screen counter (0:23–2:23). A petrol board has a small battery that runs the electronics, pumps, and starter — it needs topping up between sessions. Everything you need is in the toolkit. The one thing to get right is grabbing the correct plug inside the board. Reach in, push the clip on one side, and pull the plug out. 1:07 — Confirm it's the right one: the charging circuit always has a red cable tie . It's a female plug with two pinholes — square bottom, round top — matching the charger. If you pulled the wrong plug, the charger won't fit it. Charge 1:27 — Push the charger plug into the board's socket — it only goes one way — until it clicks. 1:39 — Plug the charger into the wall and switch the power on. 1:45 — The charger shows a red light while charging. It stays red until the board is fully charged, then turns green . 2:01 — If the battery is low, the iCU runs a balance charge based on the battery's state — it can take longer than you'd expect. That's normal; wait for green. Finish up 2:14 — When the light is green: switch the wall socket off and unplug it. 2:18 — Unplug the charger from the board, then plug the board's charge lead back into its holder where it lived. Tip: the red cable tie is your marker every time — if the plug in your hand doesn't have it, put it back and keep looking. Charging on the stand, board flat, gives you the clearance to reach past the starter. Caution: don't cut the charge short because it's "taking too long" — the balance charge is protecting the battery. Only unplug once the light is solid green, and always power the wall socket off before disconnecting. Written up by riders from the walkthrough above and our own time with these

Timestamps below follow the video's own counter (0:06–0:26). This is the cooling-system flush step from Cleaning your board after a ride . The cleaning attachment feeds a garden hose straight into the engine's cooling circuit. Use it every time you ride in salt water — it's the single most important part of the after-ride clean. Steps 0:11 — Connect the cleaning attachment to a garden-hose connector. 0:15 — Push the attachment onto the cooling pin inside the impeller and lock it with the rubber ring . 0:18 — Turn the hose on and let the water flow into the board. 0:22 — Start the engine and let it run with the water flowing for at least two minutes . Caution: don't run the engine dry for more than a few seconds — this whole procedure exists so it never has to. Difficulty: Beginner Time: ~3 min Applies to: Gas boards Last updated: Sep 2026 Watch the walkthrough Watch on YouTube ↗ · JETSURF USA — new owner series #7. Timestamps below follow the video's on-screen counter (0:26–2:00). The engine is water-cooled — water circulates around it while you ride. How you confirm it's working depends on whether your board has a catalytic converter. The telltale — boards without a catalytic converter 0:32 — These boards have a telltale : cooling water is sprayed out of a small outlet so you can see, at a glance, that the engine is being cooled. 0:39 — If you're riding and no water is coming from the telltale , head back to shore as quickly as you can so the engine doesn't overheat. 0:52 — Back on shore, check the cooling lines for wood, weed, or any debris blocking the system. Boards with a catalytic converter 0:57 — Fitted on the Adventure DFI , Adventure DFI Plus , and Cruiser — whether your board has one depends on your region and market. 1:12 — These boards have no visible telltale outlet . The cooling system still works — the water just exits at the back of the board, where the turbine exits, instead of spraying out the side. Telling a race board from a catalytic-converter board 1:29 · Race board — slightly larger exhaust, black heat surround for sound deadening, two springs, and a small black fitting at the exhaust outlet. 1:42 · Catalytic-converter board — exhaust is slightly smaller in diameter, still black, but with a stainless ring that marks it as having a catalytic converter. The cooling line on the cylinder head may also sit in a different position than on the race. Tip: learn your board's normal telltale stream — a strong steady spray — so a weak or missing one is obvious mid-ride. On a catalytic-converter board, check for flow at the turbine exit at the back instead. Caution: a two-stroke that loses cooling overheats fast and can seize. If the telltale stops on a non-catalytic board, get off the throttle and return to shore — don't keep riding to "see if it comes back." Guide One charger, one adapter, every gas board Applies to: Carbureted boards & Race / Race Titanium to 2019 Last updated: Sep 2026 The short answer The current DFI chargers use a 4-pin connector. Older JETSURF models with carburetor engines (and the Race and Race Titanium up to 2019) use a 2-pin connector. To charge an older board with the new charger you need two things: A DFI charger — the 110V/220V wall charger or the 12V charger. The 4-pin to 2-pin reduction (part A001575) — it converts the charger's 4-pin plug to the 2-pin port on your older board. Without it, the connector simply won't fit. What you need A001573 · $201.60 Charger Complete DFI 110V/220V The standard wall charger. Handles both 110V (US) and 220V (international) outlets — home, garage, anywhere with a standard outlet. Most riders should choose this one. Shop on jetsurfusa.com → A001574 · $201.60 Charger Complete DFI 12V Runs off a 12V source — car, truck, or boat. If you spend your days on the water and want to top off between sessions without heading back to shore power, this is your charger. Shop on jetsurfusa.com → A001575 · $51.45 Reduction for charger (4-pin / 2-pin) The adapter that makes it all work — 4-pin end to the charger, 2-pin end to your board. Only needed for the older boards in the chart below. Shop on jetsurfusa.com → Prices as listed on jetsurfusa.com in September 2026 — check the product page for current pricing. Does your board need the adapter? Your board Years that need the adapter UltraSport 2016, 2017, 2018 Sport (carbureted) 2019, 2020, 2021 Factory GP 2016, 2017, 2018 Race 2016–2019 Race Titanium 2016–2019 No adapter needed: all DFI models (Adventure DFI, Adventure DFI PLUS, Race DFI, Titanium DFI, Sport DFI) already use the 4-pin connector — the DFI charger plugs straight in. The normal routine is in Charging a petrol board . Not compatible: JETSURF Electric models use a completely different charging system. Neither the DFI charger nor the adapter applies to electric boards — see Charging an electric board

Each answer links to the guide that goes deeper. Choosing a board Which board should I buy first? For most people the Adventure 2 DFI — the most stable hull in the range, with dual bindings so someone else can ride it too. If you want the quick version, run the board finder : four questions and it points at one. The full reasoning is in how to choose your board . Gas or electric? Gas gives the longest sessions and refuels in minutes; electric is quiet, has no fuel to mix and less to maintain, but you charge between rides. Both are in the lineup , and the differences are laid out in how to choose your board . What are dual bindings? The board is set up for regular and goofy stance at the same time , so two riders with opposite stances can share it without changing anything. The Adventure 2 DFI, Cruiser DFI and Electric 2 have them; the Race and Titanium boards are single-stance. Bindings explained . What is a Ski board? A JetSurf ridden standing upright holding a handlebar , like a stand-up jet ski — and the handlebar comes off so you can ride it as a board. Race DFI Ski, Titanium DFI Ski and Electric 2 Ski. Re-seat it fully once the engine has cleared itself. Caution: never keep cranking a flooded engine on the starter to clear it — water doesn't compress, and you can bend the connecting rod. Turn the pump by hand and use cleaning mode. If the plug comes out wet again after a full dry, stop and check what's flooding it. See Spark plug check & replacement for reading plug condition. Tools & supplies 3 mm Allen key Two new gaskets (engine-to-reed and reed-to-throttle-body) Thread-locker (Loctite) Bright light source for the reed inspection Replacement reed valve — only if the petals fail the light check Removal 0:14 — Using a 3 mm Allen key, unscrew the throttle body. 0:14 — Remove the reed valve housing together with the throttle body. Guide Parking a board for the season Applies to: All boards Last updated: Sep 2026 A JETSURF sitting unused for weeks or months needs a different kind of care than one ridden every weekend — fuel goes stale, batteries self-discharge, and a sealed engine bay traps the moisture that causes corrosion. The steps split by power source, but the underlying idea is the same: leave it clean, leave it able to breathe, and don't let the electronics sit dead. Whatever you ride, start with a proper clean Salt water or fresh, rinse the board down before it goes into storage the same way you would after any ride — see Cleaning your board after a ride (gas) or Cleaning an electric board after a ride . If you ride in salt water, spend the extra few minutes on it — per our saltwater vs freshwater guide , most post-season problems trace back to salt that didn't get rinsed out before a board sat for months. Gas boards The short version: if you rode in salt water this season, run a full cooling-system flush before it goes away, not just a rinse — leftover salt crystallizes over a long store and is a common cause of spring corrosion. Dry the board out completely, lubricate the engine bay, pull the fuel tank and store it separately, then close the lid loosely so air can still move through — a sealed bay is what actually causes corrosion, not the cold. Start the engine occasionally during storage to keep it lubricated, and keep the battery topped up — every 30 days is a safe baseline, stretch to 60–90 in a temperature-controlled space, or check closer to 30–45 somewhere cold. The full walkthrough with every step timestamped is in Winterizing a petrol board . Electric boards Electric storage is mostly about the battery. Take it out of the board — never leave it in between long idle stretches — and charge it in storage mode rather than a full charge; that holds it around 50%, which is where a lithium battery ages the slowest. Pull the motor-bay and battery-bay covers off too and put them somewhere safe. Full steps in Storing an electric board , and the charger's storage setting is covered in Charging an electric board . Disconnect the main connector — lift the pin up , then pull the connector off. Disconnect the starter connector — push the connector case in with a finger or a screwdriver on the plastic insert, then pull it off. Unscrew the two screws on the bottom of the iron holder and lift the iCU out. Installation Set the iCU back into the holder and fit its two screws. Reconnect the starter connector , then the main connector — press each fully home, then push the main connector's pin back down to lock it. Check the bay is dry, then refit the fuel tank (see the fuel tank guide — pump wire first, then the fuel and vent lines). Power on and confirm the board activates and pairs normally before you ride. Tip: photograph the two connectors before you unplug anything. The plugs are keyed, but a reference shot removes all doubt — and note which way the main connector's locking pin sits. Caution: release the starter connector by its plastic case, never by pulling the wire. The electronics bay must be dry before you close it up — a damp iCU connector corrodes and throws faults. Here's why, and how to get it fixed. Guide Getting the right tune for your elevation Applies to: Gas boards Last updated: Sep 2026 The JEFI²S PRO — JETSURF's control unit, loaded with the engine maps. Your JetSurf's ICU comes loaded with multiple engine maps calibrated for different elevations. Air gets thinner as you go higher, which changes how much oxygen reaches the engine — so a board tuned for sea level won't run at its best in the mountains, and vice versa. What the factory maps cover The factory maps span elevations from sea level (0 m / 0 ft) all the way up to 10,000 ft (3,000 m), with adjustments for barometric pressure and ambient temperature. There are dedicated map sets for each engine type: DFI CAT DFI Alu Titanium JEFI²S-PRO How to get your ICU flashed for your elevation Find your nearest authorized JETSURF dealer. Take the ICU out of the board — full steps below. Ship your ICU to the dealer with a note stating the elevation where you ride — for example, "Lake Tahoe, ~6,200 ft." The dealer flashes the correct map for your elevation and ships it back, ready to install using the same steps in reverse. If there's one skill to focus on before anything else, it's throttle control. Get comfortable with how the board responds to the accelerator, and everything else — balance, planing out, standing up — gets a lot easier. Most of what feels hard on your first session comes down to how gradually you're getting on the throttle, not anything about the board itself. Warm up the motor before you launch Don't put the board in the water cold. Warm the motor up on land first: Insert the magnetic key into the control handle — this activates the board. Remove the key. Insert it again — this starts the engine. Let it idle for a moment, then lightly accelerate. That's your board warmed up and ready to launch. (Full pre-start checks are in Starting your board .) Get your gear positioned before you're out on the water The engine key is a wristband, and which wrist you wear it on depends on your stance — whichever foot you'll have forward, wear it on that same arm. Getting on the board and starting the engine in deep water Once you're in water deep enough — waist-deep or above — and ready to climb on: Climb onto the board and grab the handlebars and the control handle at the same time, with the control handle in your forward hand — right hand if you're goofy, left hand if you're regular. Use your other hand to take the key (the wristband) and insert it into the control handle your forward hand is holding. If the board is already active, that single insertion starts the engine. If it isn't active yet, insert the key once to activate the board, then again to start it — the same two-step sequence as the warm-up on land. What happens right after the engine starts: you'll hear the engine catch and start to rotate within 2–3 seconds. On gas boards , accelerate right away once it catches — if you don't get on the throttle in time, the engine stalls and you'll need to remove the key and run through the start sequence again.
